source.title: Sparse Semantic Dimension as a Generalization Certificate for LLMs

record.file_problem: Whole paper is present. Some typos and text-extraction artifacts occur, but they do not prevent reading the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Measures sparse SAE feature activations and tests whether their feature-index alignment matters for reconstructing LLM behavior. This bears on the LLM/SAE evidence in V4, but does not reproduce the original toy-model geometry experiments.
record.gate_note: Only V4 is tested: the paper measures SAE feature activity and reconstruction on GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B. It does not test superposition geometry, capacity competition, or feature dimensionality. Bound values and other certificate calculations are not separate rows because they do not directly measure the versions’ representational claims.
record.test_reason: The paper uses pretrained SAEs on GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B as a tool to build a generalization bound and an OOD signal, and reports only that method's performance. It takes SAE features as monosemantic units by assumption rather than testing it. It does not measure superposition geometry, capacity competition, or whether features are spread across neurons. Active-feature counts, the real-vs-shuffled loss gap and pool-mismatch rates are properties of its own certificate pipeline. The shuffled-index ablation only shows that decoder directions matter for reconstruction. It does not bear on whether the model stores sparse features in superposition.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that an SAE-based Sparse Semantic Dimension yields non-vacuous generalization bounds for GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B at realistic sample sizes. Gemma-2B needs fewer calibration samples, which the authors call a 'feature sharpness' scaling effect. Per-input active-feature count works as a runtime OOD and uncertainty signal. The shuffling ablation is presented as showing the bound is sensitive to semantics.
record.recipe_differences: Uses frozen pretrained LLMs and SAEs to measure activation sparsity and reconstruction, rather than toy networks trained to represent competing features or a direct measurement of superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model and input distribution; feature-index shuffling substantially raises reconstruction error.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a fixed pretrained SAE, per-token active-feature counts rise on random-token inputs: mean 52.02 to 78.89 for GPT-2, 60.31 to 78.33 for Gemma, with Gemma's max reaching 3840. They rise slightly on code.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE active-feature density increases on out-of-distribution inputs and can serve as an OOD signal.

fits_no_version.finding: Permuting SAE feature indices while keeping L0 and L2 fixed raises the loss gap by about 6.5 bits (GPT-2) and 8.5 bits (Gemma).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction fidelity depends on feature identity, not only on sparsity statistics.

record.problems: No independent validation that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units is reported. Feature-count statistics are distribution-sensitive; the prose and Table 3 conflict on Gemma-2B's code-versus-English sparsity comparison. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the shuffled-feature error shifts.
record.rows_left_out: Bound and risk results in Sections 5.1–5.2 and Tables 1–2 were left out because they primarily report certificate values, loss, and mismatch rates rather than directly testing the representational claims in the listed versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, no geometry, no sparsity transition.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated vs. shared dimensions.
No test of other causes of polysemanticity.

No measurement of features spread across neurons. SAE recovery and interpretability are assumed, not tested against neurons or other dictionaries; the real-SAE loss gap (0.22 and 0.50 bits) is reported only as a bound component.
Monosemanticity and stability of SAE features are asserted, not evaluated.
No comparison of 1-D vs. multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 3 text extraction is column-scrambled. The consistent reading, matching the prose, is: GPT-2 mean 52.02/59.98/78.89, std 17.69/19.31/23.58, max 165/203/419. Gemma mean 60.31/64.32/78.33, std 16.46/22.59/93.69, max 237/382/3840. The reported k values exceed the Top-k=64 setting, an unexplained inconsistency in the paper. The study cites Toy Models of Superposition only as background and assumes SAE features are monosemantic.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The paper does not measure features spread across neurons, independently establish that SAE features are complete or interpretable, or compare SAE recovery against alternative feature dictionaries.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features are not evaluated.
The paper does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Measured active SAE feature counts across input distributions.
rows.measure: Active feature count k; reported mean, standard deviation, and maximum
rows.note: The paper presents these counts as runtime SAE sparsity statistics.
rows.check: Active SAE feature counts under a fixed Top-k SAE are a property of the authors' certificate pipeline, not a test of V4. No baseline is given. The reported k exceeds the Top-k=64 cap, so the paper must be counting pre-TopK nonzeros, and it does not explain this.
